Physiology-04.question: ১) In steps of biosynthesis of thyroid hormone, TSH works on which step-
Physiology-04.option2: Formation and Secretion of Thyroglobulin by the Thyroid Cells:
Physiology-04.exp:
The correct answer is vestibular apparatus. Hair cells are specialized sensory receptor cells present in the vestibular system and inner ear, responsible for detecting balance and head movements.

Locations of hair cells:

  • Vestibular apparatus ✓

    • Semicircular canals → detect angular acceleration

    • Utricle & saccule → detect linear acceleration and head position

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Muscle ✗ → Contains muscle spindles, not hair cells.

  • Ligament ✗ → Contains proprioceptive receptors but not hair cells.

  • Joint ✗ → Contains mechanoreceptors for position and movement.

High-yield Neuro-ENT recall:

Structure Receptor
Vestibular apparatus Hair cells (balance)
Cochlea Hair cells (hearing)
Muscle spindle Muscle stretch
Pacinian corpuscle Pressure & vibration

Exam pearl:
Hair cells = sensory receptors of inner ear for hearing and balance.

Physiology-04.question: ২) Synthesis and secretion of calcitonin occur in the-
Physiology-04.exp:
The correct answer is parafollicular cells (C cells). Calcitonin is synthesized and secreted by parafollicular cells of the thyroid gland.

Key points:

  • Parafollicular cells (C cells) ✓

    • Located between thyroid follicles

    • Secrete calcitonin

    • Decrease blood calcium level by inhibiting osteoclast activity

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Perifollicular cells → Another name sometimes used for parafollicular (C) cells, but the standard exam term is parafollicular cells.

  • Leydig’s cells → Present in testes; secrete testosterone.

  • D cells → Pancreatic/other endocrine cells; not responsible for calcitonin secretion.

High-yield Endocrine recall:

Cell Hormone
Thyroid parafollicular (C) cells Calcitonin
Thyroid follicular cells T3 & T4
Parathyroid chief cells PTH
Leydig cells Testosterone

Exam pearl:
Calcitonin → Thyroid C cells (parafollicular cells).

Physiology-04.question: ৩) Excess Catecholamine causes-
Physiology-04.exp:
The correct answer is phaeochromocytoma. Phaeochromocytoma is a tumour of chromaffin cells of the adrenal medulla that causes excessive secretion of catecholamines (adrenaline and noradrenaline).

Clinical features of excess catecholamines:

  • Episodic hypertension

  • Headache

  • Sweating

  • Palpitations

  • Tremor

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Phenylketonuria ✗ → Due to deficiency of phenylalanine hydroxylase causing accumulation of phenylalanine.

  • Parinaud syndrome ✗ → Due to lesions of the dorsal midbrain affecting vertical gaze.

  • Parkinson disease ✗ → Due to degeneration of dopaminergic neurons in substantia nigra.

High-yield Endocrine recall:

Condition Hormonal abnormality
Phaeochromocytoma ↑ Catecholamines
Hyperthyroidism ↑ Thyroid hormones
Cushing syndrome ↑ Cortisol
Conn syndrome ↑ Aldosterone

Exam pearl:
Phaeochromocytoma = “5 Ps” → Pressure (hypertension), Palpitations, Perspiration, Pain (headache), Pallor.

Physiology-04.question: ৪) Hyposecretion of cortisol produce-
Physiology-04.exp:
The correct answer is Addison’s disease. Hyposecretion of cortisol from the adrenal cortex causes primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison’s disease).

Features of Addison’s disease:

  • ↓ Cortisol

  • ↓ Aldosterone (in primary adrenal failure)

  • Fatigue, weight loss

  • Hypotension

  • Hyperpigmentation (↑ ACTH)

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Cushing’s syndrome ✗ → Due to excess cortisol secretion.

  • Conn’s syndrome ✗ → Due to excess aldosterone secretion (primary hyperaldosteronism).

  • Phaeochromocytoma ✗ → Due to excess catecholamine secretion from adrenal medulla.

High-yield Endocrine recall:

Condition Hormone abnormality
Addison’s disease ↓ Cortisol
Cushing’s syndrome ↑ Cortisol
Conn’s syndrome ↑ Aldosterone
Phaeochromocytoma ↑ Catecholamines

Exam pearl:
Low cortisol → Addison’s disease; high cortisol → Cushing’s syndrome.

Physiology-04.question: ৫) Which is called master gland?
Physiology-04.exp:
The correct answer is anterior pituitary. The anterior pituitary is called the “master gland” because it secretes hormones that regulate the functions of several other endocrine glands.

Anterior pituitary hormones:

  • TSH → Stimulates thyroid gland

  • ACTH → Stimulates adrenal cortex

  • LH & FSH → Regulate gonads

  • GH → Growth regulation

  • Prolactin → Milk production

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Posterior pituitary → Stores and releases ADH and oxytocin produced by the hypothalamus.

  • Hypothalamus → Controls pituitary function and is sometimes called the “master of the master gland.”

  • Pancreas → Endocrine functions include insulin and glucagon secretion.

High-yield Endocrine recall:

Structure Common term
Anterior pituitary Master gland
Hypothalamus Master controller of endocrine system
Posterior pituitary ADH & oxytocin release
Thyroid Metabolic gland

Exam pearl:
Anterior pituitary = Master gland; Hypothalamus = Master of pituitary.

Physiology-04.question: ৬) Which hormone has receptor on cytoplasm?
৭) Which hormone is amine by chemical structure?
৮) Which promotes uterine contraction?
৯) Which hormone increases renal sodium reabsorption?
১০) Which stimulates secretion of uterine milk?
১১) Placenta not produces
Physiology-04.exp:
The correct answer is oxytocin. The placenta produces hCG, oestrogen, and progesterone, but it does not produce oxytocin.

Placental hormones:

  • hCG ✓

    • Maintains corpus luteum in early pregnancy

  • Oestrogen ✓

    • Promotes uterine growth and blood flow

  • Progesterone ✓

    • Maintains endometrium and pregnancy

Oxytocin ✗

  • Produced by the hypothalamus

  • Stored and released from the posterior pituitary

  • Causes uterine contraction during labour and milk ejection

High-yield Pregnancy hormone recall:

Hormone Source
hCG Placenta
Progesterone Placenta (after early corpus luteum phase)
Oestrogen Placenta
Oxytocin Posterior pituitary

Exam pearl:
Placenta produces hCG, oestrogen, progesterone, hPL — not oxytocin.

Physiology-04.question: ১২) Primary sex organ of male-
Physiology-04.exp:
The correct answer is testes. The testes are the primary sex organs (gonads) of males because they produce sperm and secrete the male sex hormone testosterone.

Functions of testes:

  • Spermatogenesis → Production of sperm ✓

  • Testosterone secretion → By Leydig cells ✓

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Epididymis ✗ → Stores and allows maturation of sperm.

  • Vas deferens ✗ → Transports sperm from epididymis to ejaculatory duct.

  • Seminal vesicle ✗ → Produces seminal fluid that nourishes sperm.

High-yield Reproductive recall:

Organ Function
Testes Primary male sex organ (sperm + testosterone)
Epididymis Sperm maturation & storage
Vas deferens Sperm transport
Seminal vesicle Seminal fluid production

Exam pearl:
Primary sex organ = gonad → Testis in male, ovary in female.

Physiology-04.question: ১৩) Thelarche is
Physiology-04.option2: The development of axillary and pubic hair
Physiology-04.option4: The onset of adrenal androgens secretion
Physiology-04.exp:
The correct answer is development of breast. Thelarche is the onset of breast development and is usually the first visible sign of puberty in girls.

Pubertal milestones:

  • Thelarche ✓ → Breast development

  • Pubarche → Development of pubic and axillary hair

  • Menarche → First menstrual period

  • Adrenarche → Onset of adrenal androgen secretion

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Development of axillary and pubic hair ✗ → Pubarche

  • First menstrual period ✗ → Menarche

  • Onset of adrenal androgens secretion ✗ → Adrenarche

High-yield Reproductive recall:

Term Meaning
Thelarche Breast development
Pubarche Pubic/axillary hair development
Menarche First menstruation
Adrenarche Adrenal androgen secretion

Exam pearl:
Female puberty sequence: Thelarche → Pubarche → Menarche.

Physiology-04.question: ১৪) Which of the following factor inhibits GH secretion?
১৫) Excess GH secretion during adulthood may result in
১৬) Amino acid required for thyroid hormone synthesis
১৭) Thyroid hormone increases all of the following except
১৮) Which factor inhibits hypothalamus for thyroid hormone synthesis?
১৯) Thyroid hormone deficiency in adult results in
২০) Sites of action of PTH excludes
২১) The entire period of spermatogenesis takes about -
Physiology-04.exp:
The correct answer is 74 days. The process of spermatogenesis, from spermatogonia to mature spermatozoa, takes approximately 74 days.

Additional points:

  • Spermatogenesis occurs in the seminiferous tubules of testes.

  • After formation, sperm require additional time for maturation and storage in the epididymis (about 12–14 days).

The other options are incorrect because:

  • 73 days, 75 days, 76 days → Close values but not the standard accepted duration.

High-yield Reproductive recall:

Process Duration
Spermatogenesis ~74 days
Epididymal maturation ~12–14 days
Total sperm development & maturation ~90 days

Exam pearl:
Spermatogenesis = 74 days (testicular process).

Physiology-04.question: ২২) The two testes of the human adult form up to -
Physiology-04.exp:
The correct answer is 120 million sperm each day. The two testes of an adult human male can produce approximately 120 million sperm daily.

Key points:

  • Sperm production occurs in the seminiferous tubules of the testes.

  • Requires approximately 74 days for complete spermatogenesis.

  • Production is continuous after puberty under the influence of:

    • FSH → stimulates Sertoli cells and spermatogenesis

    • Testosterone → essential for sperm production

The other options are incorrect because:

  • 110 million/day ✗ → Lower than the standard value.

  • 130 million/day ✗ → Higher than the usual estimate.

  • 140 million/day ✗ → Not the accepted physiological value.

High-yield Reproductive recall:

Parameter Value
Daily sperm production ~120 million/day
Duration of spermatogenesis ~74 days
Site Seminiferous tubules

Exam pearl:
Adult testes produce ≈120 million sperm per day.

Physiology-04.question: ২৩) Forms of calcium excludes
২৪) Tetany occurs when plasma calcium level falls below …mg/dl
Physiology-04.exp: Hypoparathyroidism leads to hypocalcemia, by decreasing the resorption of calcium from bones. Hypocalcemia causes neuromuscular hyperexcitability, resulting in hypocalcemic tetany. Normally, tetany occurs when plasma calcium level falls below 6 mg/dL from its normal value of 9.4 mg/dL.

Physiology-04.question: ২৫) Catecholamines are derived from
২৬) The most active adrenal androgen is
Physiology-04.exp:
The correct answer is testosterone. Testosterone is the most active androgen, although it is produced mainly by the testes rather than the adrenal cortex.

Adrenal androgens:

  • Dehydroepiandrosterone (DHEA) → Major adrenal androgen precursor

  • Androstenedione → Converted to testosterone and oestrogens

  • Testosterone → More potent androgen (active form)

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Dehydroepiandrosterone (DHEA) ✗ → Main adrenal androgen secreted, but has weak androgenic activity.

  • Androstenedione ✗ → Weak androgen precursor.

  • Cortisol ✗ → Glucocorticoid, not an androgen.

High-yield Adrenal androgen recall:

Hormone Key point
DHEA Most abundant adrenal androgen
Androstenedione Precursor androgen
Testosterone Most active androgen
Cortisol Glucocorticoid

Exam pearl:
DHEA = main adrenal androgen; Testosterone = most active androgen.

Physiology-04.question: ২৭) F cell of islets of Langerhans secrete
Physiology-04.exp:
The correct answer is PP (Pancreatic polypeptide). F cells (also called PP cells) of the islets of Langerhans secrete pancreatic polypeptide.

Cells of islets of Langerhans:

Cell type Hormone secreted
β (Beta) cells Insulin
α (Alpha) cells Glucagon
δ (Delta) cells Somatostatin
F/PP cells Pancreatic polypeptide (PP)

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Somatostatin ✗ → Secreted by δ (delta) cells.

  • Insulin ✗ → Secreted by β (beta) cells.

  • Glucagon ✗ → Secreted by α (alpha) cells.

Exam pearl:
F cells = PP cells = Pancreatic polypeptide.

Physiology-04.question: ২৮) Functions of insulin excludes
২৯) Insulin secretion is increased in
৩০) Diabetogenic hormone
Physiology-04.exp:
The correct answer is Growth hormone (GH). GH is called a diabetogenic hormone because it increases blood glucose levels by causing insulin resistance and reducing glucose uptake by tissues.

Effects of GH:

  • ↓ Glucose uptake by muscle and adipose tissue

  • ↑ Lipolysis

  • ↑ Blood glucose level

  • Promotes insulin resistance

The other options are incorrect because:

  • ADH ✗ → Regulates water balance and urine concentration.

  • Insulin ✗ → Lowers blood glucose (anti-diabetogenic effect).

  • Oxytocin ✗ → Causes uterine contraction and milk ejection.

High-yield Endocrine recall:

Diabetogenic hormones (increase blood glucose):

  • GH

  • Cortisol

  • Glucagon

  • Catecholamines

Exam pearl:
GH = diabetogenic hormone due to insulin antagonistic action.

Physiology-04.question: ৩১) In type-2 DM
Physiology-04.exp:
The correct answer is increased plasma glucose. Type 2 diabetes mellitus is characterized by hyperglycaemia due to insulin resistance with progressive β-cell dysfunction.

Features of Type 2 DM:

  • ↑ Plasma glucose ✓

  • Insulin resistance

  • Relative insulin deficiency

  • Usually occurs in adults (commonly >40 years, but can occur earlier)

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Low plasma insulin ✗ → Insulin may be normal or high initially due to compensatory secretion; later it may decrease.

  • Usually >30 yr ✗ → Traditionally occurs in older adults, but age cut-off is not a defining feature.

  • Normal insulin sensitivity ✗ → Type 2 DM is characterized by reduced insulin sensitivity (insulin resistance).

High-yield Diabetes recall:

Feature Type 1 DM Type 2 DM
Insulin level Low/absent Normal/high initially
Insulin sensitivity Normal Reduced
Main defect β-cell destruction Insulin resistance
Blood glucose ↑ ↑

Exam pearl:
Type 2 DM = insulin resistance + hyperglycaemia.

Physiology-04.question: ৩২) Sertoli cells are stimulated by
৩৩) Percentage of sperms in semen
Physiology-04.exp:
The correct answer is 60%. Spermatozoa contribute approximately 60% of the volume of semen.

Composition of semen:

  • Spermatozoa → ~60% (mainly from testis/epididymis)

  • Seminal vesicle secretion → ~60–70% of fluid volume (major fluid component)

  • Prostatic secretion → ~20–30%

  • Bulbourethral gland secretion → small amount

Note: Some sources describe the fluid volume contribution differently; in MCQ physiology, the expected answer for sperm proportion is approximately 60%.

High-yield Reproductive recall:

Component Main contribution
Sperm ~60% (commonly asked MCQ value)
Seminal vesicle Largest fluid contribution
Prostate Enzymes & alkaline fluid
Bulbourethral gland Lubricating mucus

Exam pearl:
Spermatozoa in semen ≈ 60%.

Physiology-04.question: ৩৪) Ovulation occurs at day
৩৫) Which hormone has receptor on membrane?
৩৬) Which hormone is not released from hypothalamus?
৩৭) Which stimulates testosterone synthesis in Leydig cells of testes?
৩৮) Which hormone has anti-inflammatory effect?
৩৯) Which promotes development of secretory apparatus of breast?
৪০) Excess ADH secretion may result in
৪১) Thyroglobulin precursor is secreted from
Physiology-04.exp:
The correct answer is RER. Thyroglobulin is a glycoprotein synthesized by thyroid follicular cells in the rough endoplasmic reticulum and then processed in the Golgi apparatus before secretion into the follicular lumen.

Thyroglobulin synthesis pathway:

  1. RER → Synthesis of thyroglobulin protein ✓

  2. Golgi apparatus → Modification and packaging

  3. Secreted into colloid of thyroid follicle

  4. Iodination of tyrosine residues → Formation of T3 and T4

The other options are incorrect because:

  • SER ✗ → Mainly involved in lipid synthesis and steroid production.

  • Golgi apparatus ✗ → Modifies and packages thyroglobulin but does not synthesize the protein.

  • Lysosome ✗ → Involved in degradation, not synthesis.

High-yield Thyroid recall:

Structure Function
RER Thyroglobulin synthesis
Golgi apparatus Modification & packaging
Colloid Storage and iodination
Lysosome Release of T3/T4 from thyroglobulin

Exam pearl:
Protein synthesis → RER; processing → Golgi.

Physiology-04.question: ৪২) Cardiovascular effects of thyroid hormone exclude
৪৩) Thyroid hormone excess results in
৪৪) PTH increase Ca<sup>2+</sup> efflux from
৪৫) Most prevalent forms of calcium
Physiology-04.exp:
The correct answer is protein-bound calcium. In plasma, the largest proportion of calcium is present in the protein-bound form, mainly attached to albumin.

Forms of plasma calcium:

  • Protein-bound calcium ✓ (~40%)

    • Mainly bound to albumin

    • Largest non-ionized fraction

  • Ionized calcium (~50%)

    • Biologically active form

    • Responsible for neuromuscular function and coagulation

  • Calcium complexed to anions (~10%)

    • Bound to phosphate, citrate, bicarbonate, etc.

  • Oxidized calcium ✗

    • Not a physiological form of calcium

Note: If the question asks for the largest biologically active form, the answer is ionized calcium; if it asks for the most prevalent bound form, it is protein-bound calcium.

High-yield Calcium recall:

Form of plasma calcium Approximate proportion
Ionized calcium ~50%
Protein-bound calcium ~40%
Complexed calcium ~10%

Exam pearl:
Total plasma calcium = ionized + protein-bound + complexed calcium.

Physiology-04.question: ৪৬) Which of the following hormones acts on its target tissues by a steroid hormone mechanism of action?
Physiology-04.option3: Antidiuretic hormone (ADH) on the collecting duct
Physiology-04.exp:
The correct answer is Thyroid hormone. Thyroid hormones act by an intracellular receptor mechanism similar to steroid hormones, mainly through nuclear receptors that regulate gene transcription.

Mechanism:

  • Thyroid hormone enters the cell

  • Binds to nuclear thyroid hormone receptors

  • Alters gene transcription and protein synthesis

  • Produces slow, long-lasting effects

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Parathyroid hormone (PTH) ✗ → Peptide hormone; acts through cell membrane receptors (cAMP pathway).

  • Antidiuretic hormone (ADH) on collecting duct ✗ → Acts through V2 membrane receptors → cAMP → aquaporin insertion.

  • β1-adrenergic agonists ✗ → Act through cell membrane β1 receptors → G-protein–coupled pathway.

High-yield Endocrine receptor recall:

Hormone Receptor mechanism
Thyroid hormone Intracellular/nuclear receptor (steroid-like mechanism)
Steroid hormones Cytoplasmic/nuclear receptor
Peptide hormones (PTH, ADH) Cell membrane receptor
Catecholamines Cell membrane GPCR

Exam pearl:
Steroid-like action = intracellular receptor → thyroid hormone and steroid hormones.

Physiology-04.question: ৪৭) Which of the following functions of the Sertoli cells mediates negative feedback control of follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) secretion?
Physiology-04.exp:
The correct answer is secretion of inhibin. Sertoli cells produce inhibin, which provides negative feedback on the anterior pituitary to reduce FSH secretion.

Mechanism:

  • FSH stimulates Sertoli cells in seminiferous tubules.

  • Sertoli cells secrete inhibin.

  • Inhibin acts on the anterior pituitary → ↓ FSH secretion.

The other important Sertoli cell functions include:

  • Support and nourishment of developing sperm cells

  • Production of androgen-binding protein (ABP)

  • Maintenance of blood-testis barrier

  • Secretion of anti-Müllerian hormone during fetal life

High-yield Reproductive recall:

Hormone Source Target
Inhibin Sertoli cells Anterior pituitary → ↓ FSH
Testosterone Leydig cells Male reproductive tissues
FSH Pituitary Sertoli cells

Exam pearl:
Sertoli cells → Inhibin → inhibits FSH.

Physiology-04.question: ৪৮) Selective destruction of the zona glomerulosa of the adrenal cortex would produce a deficiency of which hormone?
Physiology-04.exp:
The correct answer is Aldosterone. The zona glomerulosa is the outermost layer of the adrenal cortex and is responsible for mineralocorticoid (mainly aldosterone) secretion.

Adrenal cortex zones:

Zone Hormone secreted
Zona glomerulosa Aldosterone
Zona fasciculata Cortisol
Zona reticularis Androgens (DHEA, androstenedione)

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Androstenedione ✗ → Produced mainly by zona reticularis.

  • Cortisol ✗ → Produced by zona fasciculata.

  • Dehydroepiandrosterone (DHEA) ✗ → Produced by zona reticularis.

High-yield Adrenal recall:

GFR = Salt, Sugar, Sex

  • Glomerulosa → Mineralocorticoids (Aldosterone)

  • Fasciculata → Glucocorticoids (Cortisol)

  • Reticularis → Androgens (DHEA)

Exam pearl:
Zona glomerulosa damage → ↓ Aldosterone → sodium loss and hyperkalaemia.

Physiology-04.question: ৪৯) Which of the following explains the suppression of lactation during pregnancy?
Physiology-04.option1: Blood prolactin levels are too low for milk production to occur
Physiology-04.option2: Human placental lactogen levels are too low for milk production to occur
Physiology-04.option3: Blood levels of estrogen and progesterone are high
Physiology-04.option4: The maternal anterior pituitary is suppressed
Physiology-04.exp:
The correct answer is high levels of estrogen and progesterone. During pregnancy, increased estrogen and progesterone from the placenta inhibit the lactogenic action of prolactin on the breast, preventing milk secretion despite high prolactin levels.

Mechanism:

  • Pregnancy → ↑ Estrogen + Progesterone

  • These hormones promote breast development but inhibit milk secretion

  • After delivery → Placental hormones fall → Prolactin can stimulate milk production

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Blood prolactin levels are too low ✗ → Prolactin levels are actually high during pregnancy.

  • Human placental lactogen levels are too low ✗ → hPL levels are high and contribute to mammary gland development.

  • Maternal anterior pituitary is suppressed ✗ → Anterior pituitary remains active and secretes prolactin.

High-yield Reproductive recall:

Hormone Effect during pregnancy
Estrogen Ductal breast growth
Progesterone Lobule & alveolar development
Prolactin Milk production (blocked by high E/P during pregnancy)
Oxytocin Milk ejection

Exam pearl:
Pregnancy: High prolactin but no lactation because estrogen and progesterone inhibit milk secretion.

Physiology-04.question: ৫০) Blood levels of which of the following substances is decreased in Graves’ disease?
Physiology-04.exp:
The correct answer is TSH. In Graves’ disease, excessive thyroid hormone production (↑T3 and ↑T4) causes negative feedback suppression of pituitary TSH secretion.

Features of Graves’ disease:

  • ↑ T3 ✓

  • ↑ T4 ✓

  • ↓ TSH ✓

  • Autoantibodies against TSH receptor (TSH receptor-stimulating antibodies)

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Triiodothyronine (T3) ✗ → Increased due to hyperthyroidism.

  • Thyroxine (T4) ✗ → Increased due to increased thyroid hormone synthesis.

  • Iodide (I⁻) ✗ → Not the typical decreased blood marker in Graves’ disease.

High-yield Thyroid axis recall:

Condition T3/T4 TSH
Graves’ disease (primary hyperthyroidism) ↑ ↓
Primary hypothyroidism ↓ ↑
Pituitary hyperthyroidism ↑ ↑

Exam pearl:
Primary thyroid disease follows inverse T3/T4 and TSH relationship: ↑T3/T4 → ↓TSH.
